title: [Chapitre] I. Vers une géométrie des formes (topologiques) : notes manuscrites (05/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from this and the neighbouring pages). Grothendieck is axiomatizing 1-dimensional 'tame' shapes as a 'réseau': a set L of points together with a family S of 'segments' (subsets K with a two-point boundary ∂K). The axioms are F1–F6. Two structural features are used:
- A segment K with x, y in K has a well-defined subsegment K_{x,y} ∈ S.
- Each segment has a branch, or germ, at each endpoint: bor_y(I).
Two axioms are invoked:
- A gluing axiom ('axiome de recollement'): if I and J meet only at a common endpoint y and have different germs there, there is a unique K ⊇ I ∪ J with I and J as subsegments.
- Axiom F6: two segments with a common endpoint x and the same germ at x are subsegments of one segment K. Here it gives I = K_{x,y} = J.
Points are regular (L_r) or singular, and singular points are presumably finite in number (an F-axiom invoked on the next page). The stated aim, on the previous page, is to study connected, non-empty, regular réseaux.

The problem. The previous page classifies configurations of two segments I = [x,y] and J = [y,z] that 'converge' at a regular point y with bor_y I ≠ bor_y J.
- Case I, I ∩ J = {y}: gluing gives a longer segment.
- This page, Case II, I ∩ J ≠ {y}.

Case II, step by step.
1. Pick w ∈ I ∩ J with w ≠ y. Pass to the subsegments I_{w,y} and J_{y,w}, which lie in S (marked by the arrow ⇑S).
2. After renaming, reduce to two segments I, J with the same boundary ∂I = ∂J = {x,y} and bor_y I ≠ bor_y J. The marginal NB notes that w is regular except possibly when w = x = z, i.e. when I and J close up into a loop. A second NB says one will probably assume y regular.
3. Claim: bor_x I ≠ bor_x J. Otherwise F6 gives K with x ∈ ∂K and I = K_{x,y} = J, so bor_y I = bor_y J, a contradiction.
4. Claim: I ∩ J = {x,y}. Otherwise take t ∈ I° ∩ J°. Then I_{x,t} and J_{x,t} have distinct germs at x, since these are the germs of I and J. By the argument of step 3, applied at t, they also have distinct germs at t.
5. The next page continues: this produces branchings at every common interior point. Since singular points are finite, one gets a contradiction.

Conclusion. Two segments with the same endpoints and different germs meet only at their endpoints, so I ∪ J is a 'circle' (simple closed curve). This is a step toward classifying connected regular réseaux as intervals or circles: the 1-dimensional case of a tame-topology ('géométrie des formes') axiomatics.
errors: No real error. Step 3 tacitly uses that a segment K has a unique subsegment with given endpoints x, y (true for arcs), and presumably that subsegments share germs at common endpoints, i.e. bor_x I_{x,t} = bor_x I. These are presumably among F1–F5 but are not stated here.
The finiteness of singular points is only invoked on the next page; on this page the contradiction for t ∈ I° ∩ J° is not yet completed.

ideas.what: Axiomatic description of 1-dimensional tame spaces by a set of 'segments' with endpoints, germs (bor) at endpoints, a gluing axiom and a germ-uniqueness axiom (F6)
ideas.modern_name: axiomatics of tame 1-dimensional topology; arcs and germs in continuum theory; o-minimal curves
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical continuum theory (R.L. Moore, Whyburn) for arc-based characterizations; o-minimality (van den Dries, Pillay–Steinhorn, Knight) for tame topology
ideas.where_published: Tame topology programme announced only in general terms in Esquisse d'un programme (1984); this axiomatics is unpublished

ideas.what: Lemma: two segments with the same endpoints and distinct germs at one endpoint have distinct germs at the other and meet only at the endpoints, so they form a circle
ideas.modern_name: theta-curve/simple-closed-curve lemma; uniqueness of arcs with given germ
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore / classical plane and continuum topology

missed.claim: An explicit combinatorial-axiomatic framework for 1-dimensional 'formes', with segments, germs bor_x, a gluing axiom and F6, aimed at classifying connected regular réseaux (lines and circles). It is a concrete fragment of the tame-topology programme of the Esquisse that does not seem to be documented in the literature.
missed.quote: Je dis que bor_x(I) ≠ bor_x(J). Sinon, en vertu de l'axiome F6, existerait K∈S, tel que x∈∂K, et I=K_{x,y}, J=K_{x,y}
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Of historical interest: it shows how Grothendieck tried to found 'topologie modérée' synthetically, via segments and germs, rather than model-theoretically. The mathematics itself is elementary.

deep.surprise_reason: The lemma is elementary 1-dimensional topology. The only point of interest is that it documents a concrete axiomatization within Grothendieck's unpublished tame-topology project.
transcription_corrections: The case heading is 'II) I∩J ≠ {y}', not 'b)'; 'Deux cas' seems written next to it rather than struck out.
'NB On va [?] supprimer y régulier' should probably read 'NB On va sans doute supposer y régulier'.
Marginal NB: 'w régulier sauf si w ∈ {x,z}, i.e. w=x=z, i.e. si on a [loop figure with I from x to z]'.
Under 'considérons J_{y,w} ⊂ J, I_{w,y}' there is an up-arrow with S, meaning these subsegments belong to S.
